paragraphs.text:
Encomium by a Presbyter of Jerusalem on [?]

Whoever wishes to praise Dionysius would truly need a heavenly and divine tongue, one of those God-sent tongues of fire that were given to the eyewitnesses and ministers of the Word, and an angelic voice. For Dionysius revealed God. He sang the praises of the Godhead that sees all things and in perfect goodness runs through all things and holds them together, the Godhead worshipped and served in the Trinity, which is above being, above God and above goodness. He was a most theological guide to the Divine Names and to the ineffable divine mysteries. He interpreted the celestial hierarchy and praised and set in order the heavenly hosts of intellects. He was initiate, mystagogue and expounder of the ordering of the Church: its hierarchy and precedence, its sacred rites and the direction of those rites, and all the divine wisdom and beauty of Christians. Because of his pure life and his perfection in every virtue, the divine Paul entrusted him with initiation into the things shown and spoken to Paul when he was caught up to the third heaven. He was a contemporary and companion of the apostolic choir and their equal in the sacred contests. Among hierarchs he was the most holy, among martyrs the most radiant, among theologians the most [?], and among teachers the most illuminating. Therefore, O [royal] priesthood, holy nation and God-chosen assembly, I fear that by attempting the praises of so great a luminary I may [?] incur a charge of rashness [?]. For even if all the eloquence of the orators who have ever lived came together, could it reach the summit of the praises this [?] man deserves? [?] … is feeble where words are concerned. Yet I yield to the urging of your love and faith, and I will offer to God, to the saint and to you what lies within my power. For even if I fall short of the praises that befit the excellences of the one I praise and [?] …

Where, then, shall I begin my praise? Shall I follow the rules of rhetorical encomia and gather my material from things that crawl on the ground, dissolve, shift from one place to another and perish? I mean family and homeland, wealth, worldly glory and pomp. Should I gather such grounds for easily won fame and human boasting for a man who is loftier and better than all of them? Or should I rather draw on the imperishable, truly blessed and everlasting glories that he won by his excellent turning from idol worship to Christ, who is truly God, and by his gospel way of life and his athlete's contest? For what will a genealogy contribute to true glory if the parents were earthbound, wallowing in the mire and, worse, superstitious? He was counted worthy of adoption by God, the King of all. He was numbered among the heavenly ranks of angels. Together with Peter, Paul and the other heralds of God he was clothed in hierarchical and apostolic splendor. He belonged to that most blessed generation, and he was crowned with them with the diadem of martyrdom. Or what distinction could a homeland give him, however rich in horses and sheep? It might be ringed by plains, mountains, glens and ravines, thick with meadows, groves and every kind of tree and plant, encircled by harbors on the sea, watered by rivers, springs and lakes, adorned with great size, and able to show passers-by the tombs of its builders as a wonder. But he possesses the city above, Jerusalem, whose walls are inscribed on the hand of the Lord, where all who dwell are glad, and where one hears the sound of those keeping festival and the voice of rejoicing. Even so, although we said all this in our preface, judging the all-blessed man to belong among those above the world and set apart from earthly things, he was not born of obscure parents, nor was his native land undistinguished, nor was he a citizen of a mean town. What part of the inhabited world had not heard of the renown of Greece? Who does not know Athens, the boast of Greece, the famous city sung everywhere, the dwelling place of philosophers, the gymnasium and school of those greatly acclaimed for eloquence? This Dionysius came from there, and he was its most distinguished leader. He was named chief and foremost of the judges on the Areopagus. The eminence and great glory of their lineage are recounted at length by the writers of the histories of Attica, Androtion and Philochorus. From these one can infer the primacy of his ancestors and how honored and renowned they were. For among the proud Athenians he would not have been

raised to so high an office if, besides wisdom and an orderly mind, temperance, justice and courage, he had not also been adorned with the conspicuous preeminence of his family. Luke, who loved truth above all and was most wise, wrote the holy and all-wise book of the Acts of the Apostles. There he tells of those in Athens who believed through the inspired teaching and public address of blessed Paul on the Areopagus, and he singles one out: "Among whom was also Dionysius the Areopagite." This plainly shows how far this intellectual lamp excelled, both in the distinction of his family and in his wealth of virtue, knowledge, wisdom and eloquence. Luke did not say, "Among whom was a man named Dionysius," as of some unknown person. He said, "Among whom was also Dionysius the Areopagite," and so hinted that the man was on everyone's lips and very famous. Let no one think that this sacred brevity does little for the purpose of our discourse. The phrase is short, but great is the wealth that springs from it for the praise of this admirable man. In the same way Moses, who saw God, mentioned Melchizedek in one very brief passage of his account of the creation of the world. Melchizedek prefigured our spiritual priesthood, and Moses did not say whose son he was or where he came from. Yet Moses left his memory, as if on an immortal pillar, to be praised forever by later generations. Come then yourself, evangelist of the salvation and joy of the whole world, great herald of the ineffable incarnation of God the Word, most truthful narrator of his divine signs and mighty works, most detailed of the evangelists, all-blessed Luke. Come and tell us who this Dionysius is and what kind of man he was, and unfold your very concise sacred account in which you introduced this hierophant. "This," he says, "is the most renowned of the chosen men and nobles of Greece and the most eminent member of the council of the Areopagus. The office did not make him famous so much as he made the office more illustrious. He was perfect in every form of rational learning. He was the greatest philosopher among the Stoics, the Epicureans and the other philosophers. He was the most Attic and most skilled of the Atticists and grammarians, the greatest rhetorician among rhetoricians, the most contemplative of those who study astronomy, and the most exact in all the other liberal studies. Beyond all this he was complete in the four virtues. He held the scales of justice perfectly level and was the most upright of those who gave judgment in Athens. And he was all this while still bound to the religion of the Greeks, defiled with the abominations of Zeus, priding himself on the idol worship of Pallas Athena, embracing the mythical theologies of Orpheus, who drew all things after him with his music,

and delighting in Hesiod's old wives' tale, the Theogony." But then the saving grace that has appeared to all people scattered the mist of Greek folly and drunkenness and cast down all idolatrous error from the earth. Like broad-winged eagles, the disciples of our God and Savior Christ flew and ran to every part of the world and lit it up with the light of the knowledge of God. Paul came to Athens. He was the greatest of theologians, the most divine apostle of the Gentiles, the trumpet whose sound reached heaven, the chosen vessel. He trumpeted the proclamation that saves the world and brings life, and he carried the divine name of the Lord. He saw that the foremost of the Greek cities was full of idols, and he was set on fire by divine zeal. He went into the city with fervor and reasoned with the Jews and Greeks he met, learned and unlearned alike. He preached the good news of Jesus, who ransoms us from the tyranny of the deceiving, murderous dragon and from death and corruption, and he preached the resurrection of the dead. He astonished the philosophers of Epicurus and of the Painted Stoa with a wisdom that was strange, ineffable and beyond this world. He was brought to the court of the Areopagus, and there he enchanted men who surpassed everyone in philosophy. At once Dionysius left the filthy swamp of idol-madness and attached himself to Paul, who breathed a divine fragrance. He was torn away from the teachers of deceit and bound to the herald of truth. He was drawn up from the abyss of perdition and flew up to the height of salvation. He left the gloom of godlessness and came to the light of the knowledge of God. He turned away from what is truly vanity and went over to true blessedness. He renounced Belial, the broker of death, and enlisted with Christ, the cause and giver of life. He loathed the impurity of demons and embraced the purity of angels. He shook off the muddy matter of the world and took up the immaterial life. Paul rivaled the throne of the cherubim in brightness, since he had within him Christ, who rides upon the cherubim. Dionysius became a mirror able to receive the ray that flashed through Paul. Filled with the light it gave, he was illumined, and he clung to his teacher entirely, with all his soul, mind and heart. How fit this champion was to receive the apostle's light-giving exhortation! How pliant and clear was that soul, which so easily took the impressions of the archetypal seals of the gospel teachings! What a heart, which readily and without looking back broke away from every attachment of the flesh, shook off every material image, quickly believed the saving proclamation, and joined itself to Paul, who spoke the words of God, ran the course to heaven and leads people by the hand to the heavenly dwellings! What a rich and fertile spiritual field, which took the life-giving seed into its bosom and

yielded an abundant and most fruitful harvest! The weight of glory from his office and his judgeship did not make him rear back. Longing for his friends, his companions and his familiar ways did not pull him back. A tyrannical love for parents, relatives and household did not hold him. The frenzied craving for tangled riches and possessions did not bind him. Bodily pleasure did not make him slack. The [?] of a soft and luxurious life did not make him effeminate. When he heard the voice of the herald who spoke the words of God, he paid no attention to any of the things that usually delight mortals, and he hurried to join himself to Paul at once, as iron to a magnet. We admire the patriarch Abraham, who obeyed God when God commanded him to leave his kindred and his homeland and set out for an unknown foreign land, and we are quite right to do so. We also extol Elisha, who left his yokes of oxen, said farewell to his father's house, and followed Elijah, the zealot who bore the Spirit, as soon as he was called, without any delay, and this too is very just. We also exalt Philip with praises, because when Jesus, the author of salvation, called him first, he ran to him quickly and without objection, followed him eagerly, and most fittingly

How much applause, then, and what praises ought we to give this man, and with what proclamations ought we to crown him? He had not first been instructed in the law of Moses or trained in the sayings of the prophets. His ears had not been prepared by accounts of divine wonders, and he had not seen miraculous signs. Yet how readily he accepted Paul's simple word! Paul was unlettered, poor and a foreigner. His word was not dressed up with rhetorical flourishes or built on sophistic premises. Dionysius received it like seed sown in fresh soil for the first time. Without hesitating he laid it deep in his mind, and at once he brought the life-bearing fruits of the pure faith to maturity. So he almost joins the chorus of Isaiah, the most far-seeing prophet, and sings with him as he cries: "Because of the fear of you, Lord, we conceived in the womb, we were in labor and gave birth; we have brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth." Luke, the great herald, has told us these things. He is with us in the Spirit and celebrates with us this sacred commemoration of the priest-martyr. He stands as leader of the assembly that celebrates and sings of it, and he leads the praises. But we have also received things through unwritten and written tradition. We have come to set these before you, who love to listen and who are guests at a spiritual banquet. We weave them into the fabric of our praises like embroidered flowers, and we sweeten the spiritual feast with them as with spices. This, then, is the account that has come down to us, passed on from father to child since ancient times. This great Dionysius, at the time of the saving

Passion, when the earth was shaken and the sun hid its rays at midday, could not bear to see the Creator of all fastened in the flesh to the cross and tasting death, though in his divine essence he cannot suffer or be destroyed. Dionysius was utterly astonished at this wonder. Going beyond human knowledge, he understood what had happened and said: "The unknown God is suffering in the flesh, and because of him the universe has been darkened and shaken." At once he noted the time at which this world-wide wonder had taken place and kept it to himself, waiting for it to be announced later. He himself mentions that most dreadful eclipse of the sun in his letter to Polycarp. But it is better to adorn our account with his own most elegant words, as a royal diadem is adorned with the most brilliant of precious stones. For he surpassed everyone in divine speech and eloquence. Apollophanes was a philosopher and by religion a Greek. He was angry with this thrice-blessed, admirable man, the great merchant, and abused him, supposedly as his dearest friend and kinsman. He blamed him for abhorring the gods of his fathers and for preferring, pursuing and embracing the faith of the Christians, for defending it as a fighter, and for using the Greeks' own weapons against the Greeks. Polycarp was rich in the fruits of piety and virtue, and the sophist was directing his jibes at him too. Dionysius showed Polycarp how to answer the abuse and anger, and he says this: "You say that the sophist Apollophanes reviles me and calls me a parricide, because I wickedly use the things of the Greeks against the Greeks. But it would be truer for us to tell him that the Greeks wickedly use divine things against the divine, when they try to drive out the worship of God through the wisdom of God. I do not mean only the opinion of the many, who cling in a material and passionate way to the tales of the poets. Even Apollophanes himself wickedly uses divine things against the divine. He rightly calls the knowledge of beings philosophy, and the divine Paul calls it the wisdom of God. By it true philosophers ought to be led up to the cause both of beings and of the knowledge of them. And so that I may not refute anyone's opinion, whether others' or his own, contrary to what seems [?], Apollophanes, being wise, ought to have seen this: the order and motion of the heavens could never have been turned aside unless the one who is the cause of their being and holds them together moved them to it, the one who makes and transforms all things, as the holy word says. How then can he fail to worship the One whom we know from the facts as well to be the God of all, and to admire him for his power, which causes all things and is beyond words? By that power the sun and moon, with a most supernatural force and stillness, are held completely motionless together with the universe, and for the length of a whole day everything stands at the same signs." And a little further on: "Say to him: What do you say about the eclipse that happened at the time of the saving Cross? For at that time the two of us were together at Heliopolis,

standing side by side, and we saw the moon pass in front of the sun, against all expectation, for it was not the time of conjunction. And we saw it again, from the ninth hour until evening, restored in a supernatural way to its place diametrically opposite the sun. Remind him of something else as well, for he knows it: we saw the eclipse begin from the east, reach the edge of the sun and then turn back. And the darkening and the clearing did not happen from the same side but from opposite sides. Such were the supernatural events of that time, possible only to Christ, the cause of all, who does great and marvelous things without number. Say this, Apollophanes, if you are permitted, and refute it if you can, before me. I was with you then. I saw it all with you, examined it all with you and marveled at it with you." So when Paul stood in the midst of the Areopagus and spoke out with great boldness, "Men of Athens, I see that in every way you are very religious. For as I went about and looked at the objects of your worship, I found also an altar with this inscription: To an unknown god. What you worship without knowing it, this I proclaim to you," and went through all the divine discourse that followed, this most wonderful man at once received the word as though it were spoken from heaven, and he became Paul's inseparable follower. He utterly renounces all Greek rites and ordinances and abhors every kind of demonic error. He takes up the discipleship of heaven. He is instructed in the first principles of right doctrine and gospel teaching and is thoroughly taught the blameless faith. He comes to the regenerating font of life-giving baptism. He puts off the corrupt old man and puts on Christ himself, the author of life, and is formed anew. Once he was a perishable slave and a son of perishable flesh. Now he becomes a son of the sovereign Trinity, which is uncreated, imperishable and consubstantial, the cause and maker of all things, and he is made imperishable. He receives the free forgiveness of his debts. He is clothed in the most luminous symbols of freedom, adoption and sovereignty. He is counted worthy of the perfecting rite, armed with the armor of light, and initiated into the most perfect mysteries of the highest wisdom. From then on he goes out to tend the vineyard. He takes up the work of the gospel commandments and pursues the way of life that imitates the angels. He studies under Hierotheus, a man possessed by God, as his guide (Dionysius himself mentions him with praise in his theological writings), and his steps are made firm in the way of God. He enters the contests of self-control and ascetic discipline. He takes every care to keep the gift, and he hurries to offer the Giver of good things the fruits that are worthy of his goodness, the source of all good. And against the adversary of our

[?] …of life and salvation he contends. For he had been taught in the mysteries how, after Adam's sin was plunged beneath the streams of the Jordan and mortal nature was cleansed, a cleansing he won for us by being cleansed himself though he needed no cleansing, the cause and provider of all that exists went out to battle. This was the only-begotten Son of God and Word of God, without beginning and eternal together with the one who begot him, of one substance with him, the exact imprint of the Father's being and the radiance of his glory. He had shaped man after his own image and likeness. Man was then lured by the bait of the hostile serpent, the author of evil, and by the woman's mischief. He set aside the Master's commandment, was defiled by sin and slid down into corruption. Yet the Son did not overlook him. By the good pleasure of the Father and the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, through a boundless sea of love for mankind, he came down from the Father's bosom, which he never left. He fills all things and is contained by nothing. His divine descent is not to be understood as a move from place to place, God forbid! (For how could what is bodiless, unbounded and beyond understanding move from place to place?) It happened in a way that befits God. For a short time, by divine plan, he empties himself of divine glory, so that he may fill me with his divinity and I may become god by grace. He [?] the virgin womb of the unwedded, all-pure and ever-virgin daughter of David, like a seed. From her blood he formed flesh, gave it life with a rational and intelligent soul and united it to himself. He was born of her as God incarnate, twofold yet simple, with two perfect natural wills and operations. He became a mortal like us in every way except sin, yet remained without any change or confusion, and after the incarnation he is one and the same Son and one hypostasis. He came under time, he who is beyond every movement of time and is by nature the maker of all the ages. He accepted bodily growth and reached the age of manhood, he who is all-perfect and more than perfect. And he was baptized. As soon as he came up from the baptism he goes out against the deceit of the man-slaying apostate and breaks up the three-headed contrivance of his terrible wrestling holds. He throws the boastful and arrogant tyrant, puts an end to his many-sided swarm of wars and makes him easy to overcome. He shows us a pattern for the hard fight against him and gives us the [?] of valor against him…

So this noble man ordered and directed his own life by the pattern of that saving way of life. He rose up from the font of life-giving illumination, armed himself with the grace that comes from it and was anointed with the divine oil (like athletes in the wrestling schools facing an enemy battle line). At once he ranged himself against the most hostile highwayman on the road that leads up to heaven, that most cunning warrior. He laid aside the cares of this life and

became wholly a lover of the ascent to God and a contender for it. He spent days and nights in intense prayer, persevered in sleepless all-night vigils and subdued the flesh by fasting. He made the worse part submit to the better, the dust to the mind, and he thinned out the earthy grossness that tends to block the thoughts, as a gloomy mist blocks the rays of the sun. From there he was led up to the heights of contemplation and lingered lovingly on thoughts of God. He withdrew the godlike part of his soul from every material concern and lifted its spiritual eye wholly on wings toward the splendor flashing from on high. He feasted on the apostolic teachings as an eyewitness and made all of Scripture, New and Old, his breath and food. His excellence in both practical and contemplative virtue was plain to the most penetrating eyes of blessed Paul, and he was judged worthy of the rank of the hierarchy. Paul appointed him the first bishop of Athens. He was proclaimed father of his own homeland, entrusted with the first-fruits of the rational [?] and given charge of the people there who had come to believe. For it was fitting that the city which bore, raised and educated him should be the first to be adorned by its own offspring, nursling and pupil. He was the first of its children to be born spiritually to Christ, the cause of salvation, and he shone out clearly as first in every honor of life and learning. It was fitting too that the city should be guided by the pastoral leadership of its most excellent son. He brightened its godly crowns and led it to saving pastures. He settled it in a place of green grass, the smooth and unadulterated teaching, and nourished it beside the water of rest, the truly blessed final portion. O the God-decreed good fortune of the metropolis of the Athenians! How thrice-blessed it is! Truly that city is thrice-happy which bore and received such a shepherd, leader and teacher, as the Israelite people once had Moses! For here another Moses has appeared. He shot down Egypt, by which I mean the dark, polytheistic error of idolatry, not with ten plagues but with countless deadly and fiery arrows of his holy doctrines and teachings. He drowned the spiritual Pharaoh with his ruinous forces, the weed-like heretical fables sprouting from his wretched deceit, in the deep and polished waters of his all-wise divine knowledge and eloquence. Christ's chosen people were fleeing the tyranny of Beliar and superstitious worship. They trampled the raging sea of enemies of every kind who rose against them, guided by the grace that shone through him like a pillar of light and guarded by a cloud, the shelter of the all-holy Spirit. He brought them safe to the calm harbor of the blameless faith. He rose far above everything that crawls on the ground, and on the topmost lookout of the mountain of the virtues he planted the beautiful

feet of those who bring good news of peace. He entered the divine darkness, conversed with God and received the tablets of divine revelation and law. With hands raised in the shape of a cross he routed God's enemy Amalek. Some had been bitten on the heel by vipers and badly caught by the demons' ambushes and arrows, and he healed them by the Spirit of the Word. This Word was hung on the tree and put to death in the flesh, and he put to death the hostile powers. Dionysius rightly revered, worshiped and proclaimed him. He is also another Joshua. He parted the Jordan and brought the chosen people across on foot without wetting their feet, carrying the all-venerable and all-holy spiritual ark that would receive God and that was to spring from it [?]. He threw down the strongholds of the ill-named people of Jericho, the foreigners of the spirit, and of the gang of heretics. Those strongholds were shaken and overturned by his many-sided struggles for true religion, circling them again and again, and by the trumpets of sacred revelation. He held out the sunlike, illuminating word and the radiant, wise guidance supplied to him from heaven to drive out the ravenous wolves, the false teachers who ravage the rational flocks. For those being saved he secured the everlasting inheritance in the heavenly Jerusalem. That Joshua made the sun and moon stand still to help God's rescued people drive the enemy from the promised land, hurrying to give them as their portion the possession they were entering. He is also another David. David slung a stone at the fiend who boasted against God's battle line and taunted its defender, struck him down, won a most celebrated victory over the enemy and was sung with tens of thousands of shouts of triumph. Dionysius too acted bravely, with youthful vigor, strengthened by faith, hope and trust in Christ. With a courage firmer than rock he has cast down the terrible destroyer at work in the persecuting tyrants. He carried off the crown of victory and is honored without end in hymns and praises woven in countless ways. He is also another Ezekiel, a beholder and interpreter of the most mystical divine visions. He describes many kinds of divine manifestations and symbolic forms, and through images the senses can grasp he leads our understanding up, by the subtlest sacred revelations, to contemplate things immaterial and spiritual. But why should I compare so admirable a revealer of sacred things to those who only sketched the light in shadow? I ought rather to liken him to those who were counted worthy to live and speak face to face with the Light itself. He should be compared to that great Peter, chief of the apostles. To Peter the Father, who has no beginning and is unbegotten, revealed the birth of the Son, who is likewise without beginning and eternal with him, a birth before the ages and outside time, wholly beyond the grasp and bounds of every mind and word. On him, the rock, who proved an unshakable foundation of the faith, Christ, the true rock of life, maker and sustainer of all that exists,

built his own Church [?]. Christ made him the keeper of the keys to the dwelling and inheritance in heaven and the one who hands it out, giving him divine authority to loose and to bind the chains of sin. Peter lit up imperial Rome with miracles that flowed in rich abundance from Christ, and he turned the darkness of the West into the clearest brightness. Or Dionysius may be compared to the son of thunder, who thundered to the world things that are divine and above nature, beyond the reach of all human ears and minds and out of reach even of the beings above the world. For John had leaned on the breast of the true Wisdom, who is a person, and from the all-blessed and ever-flowing treasures of its hidden divine knowledge he drew up the clearest streams of theology. Or it would be more fitting still to liken him to Paul, his own guide to the light and the one who initiated him. Paul passed beyond the vaults of heaven and saw what mortals cannot see. He heard what it is not lawful to hear and was initiated into the most mystical words. He set foot in paradise, our ancient homeland, and told of the blessed life there, from which our first parents were exiled by their own rashness and their breaking of the Master's commandment. Like a bird he also crossed the whole inhabited world and took the hard-hearted gentiles captive, bringing them from unbelief to faith. Dionysius imitated these men's burning divine zeal, their sincere love, their gentleness of mind, their compassion for their neighbors, their glorious humility and their outstanding courage and boldness. He shaped his whole life to the godlike way each of them lived, and so he worthily received from the Lord the grace of an apostle, the power of signs, the light of prophecy and an ocean of theology. He made the wisdom he had gathered from Greek education a handmaid of the wisdom from above. Like a wise bee, he took the finest things below and offered them up to what is divine and heavenly. He was filled with the inspiration that pours out from the supreme divine fountain of light, and he spoke, wrote theology and composed works that astound every mind. For his reasoning soared from the study of visible things to the contemplation of invisible things. He beheld the three assemblies of the most brilliant orders above the world, and the three most holy angelic ranks within each of them [?]. As though he were himself an angel of heaven, above the world and equal in rank to the bodiless beings, he described them beautifully and set out their good order and their heavenly hierarchy. Then he reverently stretches up the light-filled part of his soul to the throne of the Godhead that is beyond God. With lips purified by the divine and most cleansing coal he speaks of the one indivisible, uncreated Godhead in Trinity: one Lordship, creator of all things, which provides for them and holds them together; one essence, one authority, kingdom and power; one will and operation; and the three hypostases in the unity,

of one substance, co-eternal and alike without beginning. They are distinguished by number and by their properties, unchangeably and immovably, yet united in Godhead. They are not blended together, but exist in one another without confusion, and each is contemplated with its own property. They are not separated by place or limit or any kind of circumscription, God forbid (for they are bodiless and uncircumscribed). They are distinguished only in thought, as far as we can conceive of counting them as three without mixing or merging them. They are served and worshiped with one service and one worship. So he teaches us to revere one God, one Lord, served and worshiped in three hypostases, with the Son and the Spirit referred back to one principle and cause. The Son is begotten before all ages from the Father alone, that is, from his essence, as the only one so begotten and in a unique way: without body, without passion and outside time. The Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, goes forth through the Son and has been made manifest to men. He teaches a single rule, a monarchy, but not one enclosed within a single person (for a one that is at odds with itself becomes many). It is a monarchy made up of equal honor in nature, harmony of will, sameness of movement, and the convergence toward the One of those who come from it. But I am like someone trying to measure the abyss with a cup when I attempt to set out, in the lowly little words of my humble self, the all-surpassing theology of this great theologian. That God-illumined book lies before us. It sends out flashes of heavenly words brighter than sunlight, which drive away the soul-destroying darkness of knowledge falsely so called and make clear and plain the security of right and divine doctrine. He pulled up by the roots the heretical quibbles and monstrous tales that the sower of weeds had sown in the apostles' time. And he also tore down from their foundations the later God-opposing blasphemies and idle chatter that sprang up against the holy, consubstantial, sovereign Trinity and against the incarnate [?] of God the Word, Christ our Savior. He did the same to those that came still later against the whole body that bears Christ's name, and against the setting up and veneration of the holy and venerable icons in the all-holy churches and apostolic sees throughout the world. Clearly God foresaw all this long in advance. Through Dionysius' tongue, sharper than any two-edged sword, he plucked up and cut off ahead of time every poisonous and destructive growth from heretical seed, and he established and confirmed the truth of the preaching and traditions of the gospel and the apostles. So we must quote word for word his most golden-gleaming divine revelation, his God-illumined and God-moved exposition about the Godhead in three hypostases and about how the only-begotten Son of God, one of the Trinity, appeared to men through his birth from the Virgin. In his exposition of the Divine Names he says this:

"Hence in nearly the whole of the theological writings we see the Thearchy sacredly praised as Monad and Unity, because of the simplicity and oneness of its supernatural indivisibility. By it, as by a unifying power, we are made one, and our divided differences [?] are folded together in a way beyond this world, so that we are gathered into a godlike unity and a union that imitates God. It is praised as Trinity because of the threefold manifestation in hypostases of its fruitfulness beyond being, from which every fatherhood in heaven and on earth exists and is named. It is praised as the cause of all that exists, since all things were brought into being by its goodness, which gives being. It is praised as wise and beautiful, because all things that exist keep the properties of their own nature unspoiled and are full of every divine harmony and holy beauty. Above all it is praised as loving mankind, because in one of its hypostases it truly and wholly shared in what is ours. It called human lowliness to itself and raised it up. From this lowliness the simple Jesus was ineffably composed. The Eternal took on extension in time, and he who in a manner beyond being transcends the whole order of every nature came to be within our nature, while what is his own remained established, unchanged and unconfused." In agreement with this is what he also writes to Gaius about the Lord's becoming man: "How, you ask, is Jesus, who is beyond all things, ranked in his essence with all men? For he is not called man here as the cause of men, but because he is truly man in his whole essence. But we do not define Jesus in human terms. He is not only man, nor only beyond being, but truly man, the one who loves mankind above all, above men and yet like men. He who is beyond being took being from the being of men. Yet he is no less overflowing with what is beyond being, he who is ever beyond being, by its very abundance. Truly coming into being, he took being in a manner beyond being, and in a manner beyond man he did the things of man. This is shown by a virgin conceiving supernaturally, and by unstable water bearing the weight of material, earthly feet without giving way, held firm by supernatural power so as not to part. Why should one go through the rest, which are very many? Through them one who sees divinely will know, in a way beyond mind, that even what is affirmed of Jesus' love for mankind has the force of a negation that points beyond. To sum up, he was not even man. This is not because he was not man, but because, coming from men, he was beyond men, and he truly became man in a manner above man. And for the rest, he did not do divine things as God, nor human things as man, but as God become man he has lived among us a new divine-human activity." And in his teaching on the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy,

setting out the meaning of the divine rite of the holy oil, he says: "So the most divine order of the beings above heaven was not unaware that the supremely divine Jesus came down to be sanctified. It understands with reverence that he lowered himself into our condition out of divine and ineffable goodness. When it sees him sanctified in a human way by the Father, by himself and by the Spirit, it knows its own Source, who in all that he does as God keeps his essence unchanged. That is why the tradition of the holy symbols sets the seraphim around the divine oil as it is being sanctified. It knows that Christ is unchanged in his truly material incarnation among us, and it depicts him so." O most blessed lips that spoke these words! Truly the gifts of the Paraclete were in them, the source from which gifts and grace have been poured out on those who are divinely purified in soul and body, and this all-holy revealer of sacred things was one of them. O tongue that revealed holy things, most fit to serve the speaking of God, which proclaimed such hidden mysteries so clearly! Truly, as the Scripture says, it proved to be the pen of a swift-writing scribe. O most luminous mind, which he who is above all mind and word lit up with such thoughts! What mind, seeing with keen and divine sight, will not see the whole most hostile host of heretics fallen and destroyed within the brief compass of these God-spoken words? It is like a crowd of wounded men amid the most dreadful cries, soaked in blood and dust. These, then, are a very few things we have gathered from the loveliest meadows of his doctrine, enough to adorn our praise of his most sublime theology and of the incomparable, most luminous orthodoxy of the true and unassailable faith. But what worthy applause could I offer for the wisdom in governing and the pastoral skill with which he directed the flock entrusted to him? He was like a helmsman who sits at the stern with his hand on the tiller and keeps a watchful lookout on every side for the onset of winds. He guards in advance against the stormy ones, which often come from far off or close at hand. He makes the sailors secure ahead of time, and before the gale strikes he slackens the sail with the forestays and lowers it. When the winds are favorable he rises up, spreads the sail again and steers the ship well. He finishes the voyage rejoicing, with the waves sounding around the keel and a following wind blowing astern. And if a stormy swell rises up somewhere, there are times when by his wise skill he lifts the vessel above the waves and keeps it from shipwreck. And if ever calm and deep stillness should lull every kind of heavy sea, even then he does not rest and sleep. He orders the rowers to drive the ship with their oars and urges them to stay alert at all times, so that the voyagers, having escaped the dangers, with their cargo…

…might bring those who sail well safely into harbour. Think of a goatherd. When destructive beasts attack, he drives them off with spears, sling and staff, and if they try to rush in at midnight, he frightens them away with torches and fiery darts. He guards the flock, going round it on every side. He leads the animals away from harmful and diseased pastures and brings them to the most wholesome and finest ones. Those that stand firm and are healthy he keeps unharmed, while he raises up the fallen, the sick, the bruised and the wounded, binding them up, anointing and healing them. Often he even tears from the claws and jaws of predatory beasts one that has been seized while it is still breathing and struggling, revives it, and brings it back, as it were, from death to life. In just the same way this most wise helmsman was called to steer the newly built Church like a ship, in the middle of the sea, with the surge rising against it on every side. He was entrusted with the oversight of a newborn flock of rational sheep at a time when the madness of idolatry held strong sway. The tyrant, together with the vain wise men and orators of the world, raged more furiously than wild beasts against those who were passing from the shadowy law-worship of the Jews, or from the godlessness of the Greeks, to the holy faith in Christ. Yet he proved himself a most highly esteemed protector, a most genuine shepherd of Christ, and truly worthy of the apostolic presidency. He cared for the people chosen by God with a mind that was protective, watchful and bold. The rabid fury of those who were openly strangers to the faith and opponents of the divine preaching he turned back by the vigour of his most pure and confident prayers, by stretching out his holy hands to God, who is able to shatter that fury, and by earnest supplications. Then there were those who in outward appearance were his own people but were disposed no better than the worst enemies, who wore a sheep's skin on the outside while within they plotted with the nature and mind of a wolf. Their malicious scheming and deceit he made plain for all to detect. As for the sophists and orators who used sophistry against the saving doctrine, employing dialectical methods and the cleverness of sophistry and rhetoric, he regarded their premises, objections and counter-arguments as a spider's web, easily undone and easily broken. He very easily tore apart and dissolved every one of their mind-stealing sophisms and puzzles. Against the enemies of the path of salvation he remained ever watchful, curbing their insolence and refuting their falsely named knowledge by the almighty power of God and of Christ our King. He made it a matter of great importance to erase from the souls he was instructing the marks of godlessness and abomination that had wrongly been stamped on them before, and to inscribe in their place the teachings of piety and of the wisdom that is above the world. Nor did he neglect, as one might suppose, to require the fruits of what he handed down and taught. Far from it: he insisted that initiation into the divine words without deeds resembles trees

that flourish with luxuriant leaves but suffer from barrenness. He taught that faith without works is dead, advising that the faithful must adorn themselves by keeping the commandments, since nothing else stands as a clearer mark of a pure and steadfast faith in and love for Christ. He was always admonishing them to fear the dreadful tribunal to come, at which each person will be required to give an account of how he has lived and what he has done. Whoever has kept the right faith, completed a life fitting for a Christian, and pleased the impartial Judge by his works will receive the everlasting delight of the truly blessed good things. But whoever did not add the best way of life and conduct to his faith, and instead defiled it with wickedness, will pay the penalty his own folly deserves, and will be punished relentlessly and [?]. For he trained and shaped everyone to walk the path of the Gospel and to live according to the apostolic tradition, distributing in due season, with discernment, the ration of grain that is the word. Those who were still infants in their condition and newly formed he fed with milk, by which I mean the simpler and more elementary teachings. Those who were mature in age and able to take solid food, having first been well purified in body and soul, he fed with perfect and mystical wisdom. He showed it more by his way of life, in his own person, becoming the finest pattern of virtue for his flock, than by teaching it in words. For since the common body of the Church was made up of many different nations, customs, ways of life and languages, this same man was a guardian who was at once simple and all-various and manifold. He was simple in uprightness and truth, free from all deceit and duplicity. He was manifold in the resourcefulness of his skilful administration and leadership, offering to each the treatment and regimen suited to him, and to those who were sick in soul he wisely and fittingly dispensed a remedy to soothe their pain, this one to one person and that one to another. Those who were running well he urged on, forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead. The sluggish and slothful, in turn, he roused to imitate those who were running well. If any sheep of the fold skipped away and wandered far off, he tracked it into the wilderness and searched all around, called it back with his pipe and his shepherd's songs, and did and endured everything until he had rescued the one that was lost. He stretched out his hand to those who were slipping from the straight path, and those lying on the ground [?]. How just were his rebukes of those who did wrong, who were insolent and who ran away from good order; how he avenged those who were wronged and defrauded by their neighbours; and how great was the love for humanity he showed toward sinners, opening the gates of repentance wide to all and receiving gladly and cheerfully, as an imitator of Christ, those who turned back, banishing from the sacred precincts, from the very beginning of the divine preaching, the inhumanity and arrogance of Novatus:

all this my discourse will show to its hearers by touching briefly on the story of what Demophilus dared to do. Those who read what the most wonderful shepherd wrote to him will learn of it more fully. This Demophilus was one of the therapeutae under the great ordainer of sacred things, Dionysius. He came from the province subject to Athens and had been appointed a therapeutes by Dionysius' all-holy consecrating laying-on of hands. This order is called that of the monks, though at that time its members were chiefly known by that other name, and they were appointed to stand at the doors of the sanctuary. This man lorded it over his own presbyter. He burst into the inner sanctuary, where it was not lawful for him to go, removed the presbyter from the altar, and drove him out of the place reserved for the clergy with dishonour and abuse. He did this supposedly out of zeal and indignation, because that Christ-imitating priest had received a man who was repenting of his sins. Demophilus regarded this man as impious and accursed and kicked him away, even though he confessed with shame that he had come for the healing of his evils and begged to obtain mercy. Having thrust him away entirely, Demophilus thought he had accomplished something great, and so, boasting, he reported what he had done to the greatest of shepherds. The most divine Dionysius wrote back to him that all-beneficial and all-wise letter, which teaches every virtue and good order. In it he made plain the indescribable compassion of our loving Lord Jesus Christ toward us, especially when we repent, and his own God-imitating sympathy, and he added an awe-inspiring story, which I shall now set before you, you who so ardently love to hear of the greatest glories of our praiseworthy father. "If you wish," he says, "I will also tell of the divine vision of a certain holy man. Do not laugh, for I shall speak the truth. Once, when I was in Crete, the holy Carpus received me as his guest. He was a man more fitted than any other for the vision of God because of his great purity of mind. Indeed, he would not even undertake the holy rites of the mysteries unless a sacred and gracious vision had first appeared to him during the preparatory prayers. He told me, then, that he had once been grieved by one of the unbelievers. The cause of his grief was that this man had led a member of the Church astray into godlessness while the days of rejoicing after his baptism were still being kept. Carpus ought to have prayed for both of them, as befits a good man. Taking God the Saviour as his helper, he ought to have turned the one back and overcome the other with goodness, and never ceased admonishing them all their lives, up to this very day, and so have brought them to the knowledge of God, so that their disputes might be settled and those who were unreasonably insolent might be compelled by lawful justice to come to their senses. Instead, though this had never happened to him before, somehow or other he worked himself up into great ill-will and bitterness, and in that bad state he fell asleep, for it was evening. About midnight, since it was his custom to wake by himself at that hour for the divine hymns, he got up, [?]

not having enjoyed undisturbed sleep, since his sleep, though long, was constantly broken. Yet as he stood for his converse with God, he was grieved and vexed in a way unfit for a holy man, saying that it was not just for godless men to live who pervert the straight ways of the Lord. As he said this, he begged God to put an end to the lives of both men at once, mercilessly, with a thunderbolt. When he had said this, he told me, he suddenly seemed to see the house in which he was standing shaken and split in two down the middle, starting from the roof. A blazing, brilliant fire appeared before him, and since the place now seemed open to the sky, the fire was coming down from the region of heaven right to where he was. Heaven itself had opened, and on the vault of heaven was Jesus, with countless angels in human form standing beside him. These things he saw above him, and he marvelled. Then Carpus stooped and looked down, and he said he saw the very ground split open into a vast, dark chasm. Before him, at the mouth of the chasm, stood the men he had cursed, trembling and pitiable, all but carried down by the unsteadiness of their own feet. From below, out of the chasm, serpents were crawling up and moving about their feet. Sometimes they coiled around them, weighing them down and dragging and pulling at them. Sometimes they bit them with their teeth or tickled them with their tails, contriving in every way to throw them into the abyss. There were also certain men in the midst who joined the serpents in attacking the two men, shaking them, pushing them and striking them. The two seemed about to fall, partly against their will and partly willingly, being little by little forced and persuaded by evil. Carpus said he was pleased as he looked down and paid no attention to what was above. He was annoyed and impatient that they had not fallen already. Many times he tried to bring it about himself, and when he could not, he was vexed and cursed them. At last, with difficulty, he looked up and again saw heaven as he had seen it before. Jesus, pitying what was happening, rose from his throne above the heavens, came down to the men, and stretched out a kindly hand to them, and the angels helped him, holding on to the two men, some from one side and some from the other. Then, with his hand already stretched out, Jesus said to Carpus: 'From now on strike me. I am ready to suffer once again for the salvation of men, and this is dear to me, so long as other men do not sin. But consider whether it is good for you to exchange a dwelling with God and the good angels who love mankind for one in the chasm with the serpents.' This is what I heard, and I believe it to be true." You have surely admired the compassion of this godly high priest toward his fellow men, no less than the goodness toward us of Christ, the truly

good and supremely divine High Priest, now that you have heard of this wonderful vision of God. And you will admire him still more if you hear of the apostolic struggles, journeys and gifts that made him so splendid that he shone throughout the whole world. For he was not only the shepherd and teacher of the Athenians, but a teacher of teachers and a shepherd of shepherds, an arbiter and a lawgiver. Nor was his course limited to Greece: it reached as far as Illyricum, like that of Paul, his guide and the one who ordained him. Having received apostolic grace and the power of signs, he hurried everywhere like a winged creature, in the manner of the apostles, preaching the Gospel of true life. With apostolic seines and all-catching nets he caught alive and took captive those held in the darkness of error, drawing them out of the depths of ignorance into the light of truth. That he gave counsels for teaching and mystical instruction, like a teacher and another chief apostle, to those entrusted with leading and teaching churches in various lands and islands is plainly proclaimed by the doctrines, mystagogical teachings and ordinances he addressed to the most holy bishops of the Ephesians, the Smyrnaeans and the Cretans, namely Timothy, Polycarp and Titus, who had been ordained as prelates by the very foundations of the most holy Church, I mean the apostles. That he also completed an apostolic course and was glorified by God with extraordinary miracles will be confirmed by many other things, which my discourse will go through as it proceeds to recount the martyr's contests he endured so steadfastly. Above all it is confirmed by the cloud that snatched him up from the western region and lifted him aloft. Like the most exalted apostles, who had seen God and spoken of God, it carried him through the air, each from a different end of the earth, and brought him suddenly to the all-venerable Jerusalem, the common mother of all Christians. There, in Zion, the citadel of the divine mysteries and the mother of the churches, it united him with the disciples of Christ at the time when the body of the all-pure Mother of God was being buried. Her body was honoured by the descent and presence of God the Word, who had ineffably taken flesh and been born of her, and it was escorted by the angelic ranks who walk in heaven. It was carried from Zion to Gethsemane, her sanctuary that imitates heaven, on the all-holy and divine heads and arms of the apostles, and it was hymned and glorified by tongues of fire, moved by the Spirit and supremely skilled in speaking of God. From there, after being laid in the tomb, she was taken up whole into the realm above the heavens, she who is higher than all the heavenly powers and is mistress of all
We must hear it from this revealer of God himself as he tells of it, for there could be no more trustworthy witness of that angelic choir, the equal of the angels, of

that gathering borne on the clouds: "And indeed we have also been very careful never to undertake to repeat what our divine guide himself clearly set out in his exposition when explaining the same scriptural saying. For even among our divinely inspired hierarchs themselves, when, as you yourself know, we and many of our holy brothers came together to behold the body that was the source of life and had received God, and James the brother of God was present, and Peter, the chief and most venerable summit of the theologians, it then seemed good, after beholding it, that all the hierarchs should hymn, each as he was able, the infinitely powerful goodness of the divine weakness. On that occasion, as you know, he surpassed all the other initiates in sacred things after the theologians. He went wholly out of himself, was wholly carried beyond himself, and experienced communion with the things he was hymning, and by all who heard and saw him, whether they knew him or not, he was judged to be possessed by God and a divine singer of hymns. What should I tell you about the things said of God there? For unless I have even forgotten myself, I know that I have often heard from you some parts of those inspired hymns." Let no one, beloved, disbelieve this account. Let him consider Cornelius and those with him: they too, like Peter, John and James and their companions, were filled with the fiery grace of the all-holy Spirit, spoke in tongues and received a share in wonder-working power. For how could men scattered in every direction, each appointed to govern a diocese in a different place and to carry out a mission, have gathered together all at once in a single instant, unless each of them had been granted a divine cloud-like [?]? Indeed, to all who came to the true faith at the beginning of the saving preaching, and were enlightened by the divine illumination itself, the Spirit who bestows supernatural gifts and is the source of good richly distributed various kinds of tongues, gifts of healing and workings of various mighty powers. How much more, then, to those like the great apostolic Dionysius! But the sacred trumpet of his victorious martyrdom has sounded in due season and urges us to enter upon and behold his divine contests, and it moves my discourse on to the praise of his most glorious feats. Before we step onto the threshold of the martyr's arena, however, this audience, so eager to listen, must know that, following the divinely inspired writings of the herald of God and holy martyr whom we are praising, we have concluded that his blessed contest took place in the last years of Trajan's reign. He says this in the fourth chapter of the treatise On the Divine Names, where he sings the praises of the name "yearning love" (eros): "And indeed it seemed to some of our writers on sacred things that the name 'yearning love' is even more divine than the name 'love' (agape). And the divine Ignatius writes: 'My yearning love has been crucified.'" For Ignatius the God-bearer wrote this saying when he was about to contend as a martyr in Rome

and to be thrown to the lions as food by order of the tyrant Trajan, around the ninth year of his tyranny, when Trajan had raised a persecution against the most pious Christians. Ignatius wrote it in his letter to the Romans. From this it can be inferred that Dionysius, the revealer of sacred things, suffered martyrdom toward the end of the persecutor's tyranny, as we have already said. He also wrote to the son of thunder, the thrice-blessed John, who thundered and spoke of God most loftily, beyond all understanding, of things both within the world and above it. John was then confined on Patmos by sentence of Domitian, who reigned after his brother Titus (both were sons of Vespasian) and who raged against the faithful around the last year of his reign. Dionysius says, foretelling it prophetically (for he shared also in the grace of prophecy): "On the contrary, nothing will deprive us of the all-radiant beam of John. For now we shall meet it in remembering and renewing your true theology, and a little later (I will say it, bold though it is) we shall be united with you yourselves. And I am entirely to be trusted, for I have learned what has been foreknown from God and I say it: you will be released from your confinement on Patmos and will return to the land of Asia, and there you will produce imitations of the Good and hand them down to those who come after you." Not long afterward, then, Domitian died, just as the divine Father, distinguished by apostolic and prophetic gifts, had foretold, and Nerva, succeeding to the throne, recalled those in exile. At that time the greatest of the evangelists also returned to Ephesus, the metropolis, and the prediction received [?]

When Nerva departed this life, having held the reins of Roman rule for one year, power passed to Trajan the tyrant. He was greatly elated by his victory over the Scythians, the Thracians and very many other nations. He thought he ruled over nothing unless he also brought the most pious community of Christians into subjection to the worship and veneration of demons and abominable idols. So he fanned the flames of a most savage persecution and made the whole land under his rule drunk with the blood of martyrs. He sent out the most merciless persecutors in every direction to compel all Christians, without restraint, to sacrifice to the idols, or, if they would not obey, to put them to death with every kind of torture. Now the blessed Dionysius, thrice blessed and many times over, had for seventy years passed through countless reproaches, battles and dangers from his own countrymen, and at times from those who had once shared his religion and from the companions of his youth, or rather from fools. He had stood in battle against such great multitudes of barbarians and idol-mad Greeks, and against the most savage dispersion of the lawless and hostile Hebrews. He had run a course twice as long as the one run by Paul, who endured so many contests and whose course led to heaven, at least as far as the length of time is concerned. And countless peoples, through the signs and wonders [?] performed by him through the working of the all-holy Spirit,

…[?] having netted them into faith in the one Christ, he passed through the very long and very harsh stretches of the first persecution. Nero stirred that persecution up against the whole body of those who bear the name of Christ. He was the first of the persecutors, the worst of all who have ever reigned and the most profane, and he put to death the chief disciples of Christ. Later Dionysius bravely endured the storms that Domitian's madness brought on the faithful as well. He proved himself tested in all things and won widespread fame. So winged rumour, running everywhere, sounded his celebrated name in Trajan's most savage ears. It thundered the news of the swift apostolic course he ran everywhere, his great sweat and toil, and his power in deed and word. Through these the most divine and saving faith he preached was confirmed and spread by signs and wonders that he worked in marvellous ways, and the superstition of the Greeks and their idol-worship were openly denounced and overthrown by force. The raging tyrant was greatly disturbed by this. He sent men of bestial mind into the regions of the setting sun to track down and hunt the herald of God. These men surpassed even Phalaris and Echetus, who are notorious for savagery, mercilessness and cruelty. If they found him anywhere and he yielded to the imperial decrees and agreed to worship the demons and sacrifice to them, they were to load him with honours and bring him back under escort. If he refused, they were to punish him on the spot with the sword.

The devil's servants were spurred on by the tyrant's most godless commands. Like horses driven by a gadfly, or hungry beasts rushing to the hunt, they raced through the land of Gaul. There they gathered a crowd of common and [?] men and searched for the all-renowned revealer of God. When the persecutors were told that he was in Paris (a small town of that name), they rode there at full speed. They found him driving out the error and darkness of idol-madness by preaching the truth, by the radiance of divine teaching, and by the prodigies of his miracles. The eyes of the blind received their sight and the ears of the deaf were opened. The tongues of those who stammered were loosed and the steps of the lame were made firm. Those suffering from various diseases were set free by calling on the almighty Saviour. His most wonderful servant worked these marvels and called those sitting in the darkness of ignorance to the light of knowledge and salvation. Because of this the number of the faithful grew, and churches to God were built throughout Gaul and Germany, that very great province. The number of the superstitious shrank, the precincts of the idols were thrown down, and the rule and deceit of hostile Beliar was trampled underfoot and led away in triumph. The wretch could not bear to see his [?] power destroyed, and so he drove his subjects and servants into a frenzy

against the saint who was overthrowing his authority and making a public example of his shame. They seized him furiously together with his most holy disciples and spiritual sons, Rusticus and Eleutherius. He had consecrated one of them as a priest and the other as a deacon. Both had shared the contest and the race with their own leader and enlightener, as Silvanus and Timothy did with Paul, the light of the world. The persecutors sat on the tyrant's tribunal. With a dragon's glare and a lion's roar they asked him: "Wretched old man, are you the one who forbids the worship of our gods? Are you the one who uses magic arts, eloquence and sorcery to persuade the peoples not to serve them, who opposes the invincible emperors and the [?]…? What do you call yourself? What is your religion, and what god do you preach?" He was not in the least afraid of their insolent madness and answered very boldly: "I am the destroyer of your godlessness, the overthrower of idolatrous abomination, and the denouncer of all Hellenic error. I have been appointed by the power of Christ, the only-begotten Son of God. I have dedicated myself to him as his slave, and I serve him in my spirit. Before all ages he was begotten of the Father, without passion and outside time. At the end of the ages he became flesh and was born of the Virgin Mary, without seed and without corruption. He became a mortal like us in all things except sin. Through his own cross and death he abolished the power of the devil and put death to death. He went down even to gloomy Hades and dissolved the darkness there. By his resurrection from the dead on the third day he made light shine on the world and poured out life and incorruption. He taught us to worship one God in three hypostases, distinct without confusion: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. He himself is one of the uncreated Trinity, coeternal, equally without beginning, and of one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit. This is the true God we preach. This is the pure and blameless faith of Christians that we proclaim. For it we are ready to suffer anything. We fear neither fire nor sword nor the rage of wild beasts, nor any kind of torture you can devise." The tyrants were astonished at the daring of the most courageous and learned old man. Breathing threats and raging, they spoke again to him and to the disciples who shared his struggle: "So you despise the decrees and commands of our emperors and rulers, and disregard the honour and authority of our unconquered gods?" The divine hierarch, who led the battle line of the martyrs in word and deed, answered even more boldly: "May every impious command of emperors and rulers that opposes God perish! And may the gods who did not make heaven and earth per-

ish, for your gods are truly powerless, wretched and abominable, and worth nothing. They are demons, figments of an ill-starred mind, and the handiwork of human hands. May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them: deaf, blind and without sense. We know that Christ is truly God and Creator of all things, their guardian and the giver of life. Him alone we worship and preach, in him we place our hopes, and for him we are eager to die. We count ourselves as sacred victims and offerings. As we hurry toward this slaughter we rejoice greatly, because we firmly believe that we will rise again. We will receive the better, more blessed and everlasting portion and be crowned with unfading crowns. But people like you do not believe in him. You reject his divinity and his true, eternal and endless kingship, and you kill his servants. We will see you handed over to eternal fire and to incurable, unending torments." At this the most wicked and impious persecutors were shaken. Filled with anger and rage, they gnashed their teeth and drew their swords. The thrice-blessed herald of God readily stretched out his neck, and they cut off his divine and all-holy head. After that they also cut off the heads of the pair who had been his companions, fellow runners and fellow athletes, and no less his fellow preachers. Each was eager to reach the arena of the martyr's contest, and of perfection by beheading, before the other. They cheerfully put out their necks and offered them, comely, to the stroke of the sword. They did not want to be left far behind their tutor and initiator in this perishable and thorny life. They wanted to depart with their teacher and guide quickly and in the same way to the judge of the contest. They had shared his contests, and so they hoped to share the same crowns and prizes. They had been well trained and already exercised in many athletic contests of every kind. They had Christ himself as their divine love. Through all this they were taught to spare neither body nor soul, so that they might delight in him alone, who is clearly the tree of life. How then could they fail to emulate their trainer and teacher in a martyr's valour? [?] A mighty general fights in front of his army, encourages his comrades, urges them to raise the war cry, and is the first to engage the enemy's forces. In the same way the old man, most experienced in divine contests, who had reached a deep and rich old age, leapt ahead to the most blessed slaughter for Christ. He carried off the crowns of victory first, and he prepared his sweetest sons to follow him and gladly choose the same all-blessed death. Who, then, could admire him as he deserves? For seventy years he walked the apostolic road and preached Christ the Saviour. He sowed the noble and pure seed of the saving word in many fields of rational souls,

reaped an abundant harvest, and stored very genuine and precious fruits in the sacred granaries. Who could praise as much as he would wish the one who excelled for so long in the way of the gospel? He emerged victorious in the midst of tyrants who fought against Christ and of a hostile people more savage than lions and wolves. What tongue could tell his virtues, achievements and contests? The tribes of the earth were amazed at them. The ranks of the heavens extolled them as divine. Christ, King of all and giver of prizes, accepted them. He crowned the one who had achieved them and contended to the end with proclamations of victory and with the reward of most brilliant crowns. O holy and divine head, cut off for Christ, who is Love itself! O all-holy head, which held very many and very great divine and ineffable things that the world could not hold, and which fought countless long contests for the divine preaching! O head that walked among the orders above the heavens, and understood and uttered things at the very limits of all speech and thought! O that most divine soul, which flew up with an angelic escort to the vaults of heaven! It rose in glory to Jesus, the Lord of glory and giver of crowns, to receive the reward of its glorious labours. Each of the powers above the world sang its praises. They honoured its contest and repaid the angelic hymnody that their common hymn-writer had composed with divine inspiration and perfect harmony. The Jerusalem above opened its gates and took this soul into its bosom. The Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven embraced it. The spirits and souls of the righteous, the holy and the humble of heart also took it in their arms. This soul had lived in righteousness and holiness, with modesty and a godly kindness. It had boldly confessed the faith to the point of blood and fought for it. The choir of the apostles fittingly gloried in it. The company of the prophets rejoiced over it. The festal assembly of the prize-bearing martyrs celebrates and rejoices with it, clothed and adorned in the royal purple that it wove and dyed from its own contests and blood. Blessed, then, is the city that has kept as its treasure your God-crowned and most venerable head and your precious relics. It also keeps the relics of your fellow disciples, whom you offered to God as wholly blameless sacrifices and as most fragrant incense. O best of the heralds of God, of hierarchs and of martyrs! Your holy blood has reddened that city, and from it healing and springs flow forever for those who take refuge there in faith and ask to be healed of painful diseases. Truly blessed is Paris. It is smaller than the other cities of Gaul, but it has become more illustrious because it obtained you, O foremost of teachers. You are a treasure more precious than all visible wealth, and the city has you as its patron and the guardian of its citadel. For God gave you to it as its sanctification. You sanctify the Christ-loving gathering of its citizens and visitors, and

you are its spiritual wealth. You provide a delight that does not increase the body's bulk, sweeten the throat for a moment, and then quickly perish and fade away. That is the kind of delight that land and sea provide, and the [?] gulf, and the deep, fish-filled river that flows around the city and roars about it, rivalling the sea-like streams of the Nile. You stand in front of the city as a very strong wall. It is not fitted and built of rough and polished choice stones, or propped up with bulwarks, towers and battlements like an iron enclosure. It is founded on your holiness and that of your fellow athletes, and its towers are your acceptable intercessions before God. These bring down fire from heaven, which consumes godless captains of fifties, hundreds and thousands together with their barbarian armies. You lie before the city as a harbour of salvation. You receive those who put in from the storm of life and keep every kind of misfortune away from them. Your most holy shrine has been planted in the city like a spiritual meadow, like the paradise in Eden. Through the grace that dwells in it, it gives the faithful every kind of refreshment. It sets out a table full of every sort of spiritual food, which feasts souls, makes them flourish, and gains them incorruptible life. With boldness [?], then, you stand at the divine, heavenly and spiritual altar with your fellow crowned ones [?]. There you appeal on behalf of the whole world to the gracious Jesus, the true God, high priest and giver of crowns, the cause and source of all goodness. You loved him and preached him, and for his sake you were beheaded and rightly received the crown. Watch over, care for and bless those now gathered at this sacred and venerable festival of yours. They are festively celebrating your most beloved memory and singing and honouring your contest, which is worthy of honour. Most divine high priest and most illustrious of martyrs, appeal to the compassionate God and intercede with him. Ask him to lift from us the burden of the violence that surrounds us, to end the tyranny over us, and to drive away the gloom that floods over us. Ask him to grant calm and deep tranquillity to the churches and a state of peace. Then, with peace prevailing and with one harmony and agreement in divine doctrine holding sway, Christ, the true chief shepherd and prince of peace, may be glorified by all with one mind. To him belong all glory, honour and might, together with his Father, who has no beginning and is of one substance with him, and his all-holy, good and life-giving Spirit, now and always and to the endless ages of ages. Amen.
